title: Manhattan Distances of All Arrangements of Pieces
statement:
Put `k` identical pieces on a grid of `m` rows and `n` columns, each piece on a cell of its own. Because the pieces are identical, an arrangement is simply the set of `k` cells they occupy, and every such set counts once.

For one arrangement, add up the distance of every pair of its pieces, each pair once, where pieces at `(r1, c1)` and `(r2, c2)` are `|r1 - r2| + |c1 - c2|` apart (their Manhattan distance). Return the sum of these totals over all possible arrangements, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
signature: int distanceSum(int m, int n, int k)
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all C(mn, k) arrangements is hopeless, so swap the order of the sum: go through pairs of cells and ask how many arrangements contain both. Two fixed cells hold pieces, and the other `k - 2` pieces take any `k - 2` of the remaining `mn - 2` cells, so every pair of cells is counted exactly C(mn - 2, k - 2) times. The answer is that count times the total distance over all pairs of cells.

That total splits into rows and columns. Two rows `d` apart can be chosen in `m - d` ways, and each choice pairs `n` cells with `n` cells, so the row part is n² · Σ d(m - d) = n² · (m - 1)m(m + 1) / 6. The column part is the same with `m` and `n` swapped.

## Approach

1. Compute `rowDistances` and `colDistances` with those formulas, exactly, in BigInt; `pairDistances` is their sum modulo `MOD`.
2. Set `others = m · n - 2` (cells left once a pair is fixed) and `extra = k - 2` (pieces still to place).
3. Build C(others, extra) as a product: `numerator` multiplies `others - extra + 1` up to `others`, `denominator` multiplies 1 up to `extra`, both modulo `MOD`.
4. `MOD` is prime, so dividing means multiplying by `power(denominator, MOD - 2)`; the result is `ways`.
5. Return `pairDistances · ways` modulo `MOD`, as a Number.

## Example 1, step by step

`m = n = k = 2`. `rowDistances = 2² · (1 · 2 · 3) / 6 = 4`: four of the six cell pairs lie in different rows, one row apart. By symmetry `colDistances = 4`, so `pairDistances = 8`. Then `others = 2` and `extra = 0`, the loop does not run and `ways = 1`, since each arrangement is just one pair. The answer is 8.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k + log MOD): one loop builds the binomial coefficient and one fast power inverts it.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Divide by 6 before reducing modulo `MOD`: the exact product is a multiple of 6, but its remainder need not be.
- A product of two values below `MOD` can reach 10^18, beyond 2^53, so JavaScript needs BigInt; Java and C can use 64-bit integers.
- `k = 2` and `k = m · n` both give `ways = 1`; make sure `extra = 0` and `extra = others` work.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | 10^9 + 7, as a BigInt |
| `power` | modular power by repeated squaring, used for the inverse |
| `rows`, `cols` | `m` and `n` as BigInts |
| `rowDistances`, `colDistances` | sums of row gaps and of column gaps over all pairs of cells |
| `pairDistances` | total Manhattan distance over all pairs of cells, modulo `MOD` |
| `others`, `extra` | free cells and remaining pieces once a pair is fixed |
| `numerator`, `denominator` | the two products that make C(others, extra) |
| `ways` | arrangements that contain a given pair of cells |

narration.3: power(base, exponent) raises base to exponent modulo MOD by repeated squaring.
narration.6: When the exponent's lowest bit is set, this power of base is part of the result.
narration.9: Square the base for the next bit of the exponent.
narration.16: Row gaps over all pairs of cells: rows d apart can be chosen m - d ways, each pairing n cells with n cells, and the sum of d(m - d) is (m - 1)m(m + 1)/6.
narration.17: The same count for column gaps, with m and n swapped.
narration.18: The total distance over all pairs of cells, reduced modulo MOD.
narration.19: Once two cells hold pieces, this many cells are left for the others...
narration.20: ...and this many pieces still need a cell.
narration.23: Build C(others, extra) as the product of the fractions (others - extra + i) / i.
narration.24: Multiply the next numerator factor in, modulo MOD.
narration.25: Multiply the next denominator factor in, modulo MOD.
narration.27: MOD is prime, so denominator^(MOD - 2) is its inverse; ways counts the arrangements containing any one pair of cells.
narration.28: Every pair of cells is counted ways times; turn the result back into a Number.
